question: Will Squamish property taxes go up in 2027?
short: Will Squamish property taxes go up in 2027?
answer: Very likely, yes. District staff's draft 2027 budget needs 10.4% more property tax revenue than 2026. That works out to about $342 more for an average home, before any extra items council decides to add. The new council still has to approve the plan, and the final number is not set yet.

p.t: Staff presented the General Fund operating budget to council on September 29, 2026. The base plan needs 10.4% more property tax revenue in 2027 than in 2026. Staff say that is about $342 more for the average home, measured against an average 2026 municipal tax of $3,294.

That 10.4% does not include extra services that were still waiting on council approval. Staff priced those at another 1.7% (about $56 for an average home) for added service and up to 1.2% for one time projects. At the September 29 meeting, council kept most of the extra services but cut two items worth $123,000 and $58,000, and sent a $580,000 community safety package back for more work. No updated total has been published.

after.t: This is the increase in the total tax the District collects, not a promise about your own bill. Your bill depends on how your assessment changed compared with others in your neighbourhood and property class.

p.t: Staff list the main costs. Wages and benefits under existing union and staff contracts add 2.2%. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police contract adds 1.1%. Higher debt payments, mostly for the new Public Works Facility, add 1.8%. Transit adds 0.5%, and the Cheekye debris flow barrier reserves add 0.5%.

Staff also kept setting aside $7.2 million, equal to the general tax paid by a single large business, for one time spending like capital projects instead of day to day operations. This follows the District's tax policy of not relying on one taxpayer for ongoing costs.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police: 1.1%

p.t: Squamish adopted its first ten year financial plan (2026 to 2035) on January 13, 2026. That plan predicted a 13.0% tax revenue increase for 2027 and 12.9% for 2028. The new draft is lower for 2027, but staff still forecast 12.7% for 2028 and 7.9% for 2029.

after.t: Staff say the 2028 jump comes from new police positions that were partly covered by a reserve fund until now, plus more borrowing for the Mamquam Bridge deck, the Xwu'nekw Park sea dike and Squamish River dike raising.

sections.h: Water, sewer and garbage fees for 2027

p.t: Utility fees are billed separately from property tax. Staff recommended a 1.8% rise for water and 8.8% for sewer, and proposed 10.3% for curbside garbage.
On September 22, 2026, council approved water at 1.8% and sewer at 8.8%, and lowered the garbage increase to 8.3%. These rates still need to go into the fees bylaw before they take effect.

Council held budget workshops on September 8, September 22, September 29 and October 6, 2026. The new council took office on November 3. The District says a workshop to introduce the plan to the new council and a public information night are coming, but the dates had not been posted as of November 9.

The 2026 plan was adopted in January, so the final 2027 number may not come until the new council votes in the coming weeks. Tax rates themselves are set in the spring, after BC Assessment releases its revised roll.

The District posts every budget report and its online budget book on Let's Talk Squamish, where you can answer its questions about what matters most to you. You can also email budgetfeedback@squamish.ca at any time. Feedback goes to the new council, and the District will publish a What We Heard report.

faq: Are property taxes going up in 2027 in Squamish?
Almost certainly. The draft budget needs at least 10.4% more property tax revenue than 2026, about $342 for an average home, before extra items council adds. Council has not adopted it yet.
How much did taxes go up in 2026 and 2025?
The 2026 increase was 12.8%, adopted January 13, 2026. The 2025 increase was 12.5%.
Will my own tax bill go up by exactly 10.4%?

Not necessarily. That number is the increase in total tax collected. Your bill depends on how your assessment changed compared with others in your property class. New construction also spreads the cost over more properties.
When will the 2027 budget be final?
The District has not posted the date yet. The new council has to vote on the financial plan, and tax rates are set in the spring of 2027.
How can I give input on the 2027 budget?
Use letstalksquamish.ca/budget-2027, email budgetfeedback@squamish.ca, or attend the public information night once its date is announced.

question: How much do the Squamish mayor and councillors get paid?
answer: In 2025 the District of Squamish paid Mayor Armand Hurford $103,946 and most councillors $46,926 each, before expenses and benefits. By June 2026 the base pay was $106,193 for the mayor and $44,813 for a councillor. A bylaw council gave three readings on September 29, 2026 sets the pay at $125,000 for the mayor and $45,000 for each councillor starting in 2027, which covers the new council led by Mayor Sean Easton.

sections.h: What each member was paid in 2025

p.t: Every year the District must publish a Statement of Financial Information that lists what each council member was paid. The 2025 report, page 40, shows the amounts below.

after.t: Members who also sat on the Library Board or the Squamish Sustainability Corporation board were not paid extra for those seats.

p.t: Pay is set in the Remuneration and Expenses Bylaw No. 1503, first adopted in 1998. Before the 2026 change, it set the mayor at $85,421 as of January 1, 2019, with a raise every January that follows the District's pay policy for its non union managers. Councillors get a fixed share of the mayor's pay, 42.2%. The acting mayor rate is 60% of the mayor's pay.
A staff memo explains that the yearly raise for council matches the raise for those staff, and that raise is partly based on the consumer price index, a measure of inflation.

sections.h: The 2026 pay review and the 2027 raise

p.t: On December 9, 2025, council moved $4,000 a year out of its contingency budget so that a pay review costing $15,000 to $20,000 could be done every four years, timed with elections. The District hired Western Compensation and Benefits Consultants, who surveyed 11 municipalities.
The review found Squamish pay slightly below average. The surveyed places paid mayors an average of $116,550 and councillors $45,479, while Squamish paid $106,193 and $44,813.

Bylaw 3285 raises the mayor's pay to $125,000 as of January 1, 2027 and lowers the councillor share from 42.2% to 36%, which works out to $45,000. Pay then goes up for cost of living each January. The bylaw also adds life insurance to the listed benefits and lets members claim up to $2,000 a year for legal costs. It was set for adoption at the October 6, 2026 council meeting.

list: Councillor: $44,813 in 2026, $45,000 from 2027 (almost no change)

sections.h: How council voted on its own pay

p.t: At the July 14, 2026 Committee of the Whole meeting, Councillor Hamilton moved and Councillor Greenlaw seconded the plan for a $125,000 mayor and a 36% share for councillors. Mayor Hurford and Councillor Andersen tried to raise the share to 40%, which would have meant about $50,000 for each councillor. That change failed, with Councillors Hamilton, Greenlaw, Pettingill and Stoner opposed. The main motion carried. A proposal for up to $2,000 a year for legal costs also carried, with Councillors Stoner, Andersen and French opposed.

Council approved both ideas on September 1. On September 22 it reworded the legal costs item to cover legal fees related to council work. On September 29 the bylaw got first, second and third reading, moved by Councillor Hamilton and seconded by Councillor French.

sections.h: Expenses, benefits and the old tax break

p.t: On top of their pay, members get travel costs back when they travel outside Squamish for District business: hotels at cost, the federal government's rate per kilometre for driving, and a $75 daily meal and small costs allowance with no receipts needed. The District pays for health, vision and dental coverage, accident insurance and the employer share of the Canada Pension Plan. Pay can be cut by 10% to 25% for a year if a member is found to have broken the code of conduct.

The bylaw still says one third of each member's pay is an allowance for small costs of the job. That one third used to be tax free, but the federal 2017 budget made allowances like this taxable starting in the 2019 tax year.

sections.h: How Squamish compares with nearby places

p.t: These are 2025 amounts taken from each place's own financial report. North Vancouver District members are also paid separately for regional board seats, and that is not counted here.

faq: How much does the mayor of Squamish get paid?
$103,946 in 2025 and $106,193 a year at 2026 rates. From January 1, 2027 the mayor's pay rises to $125,000 under Bylaw 3285, then goes up with cost of living each January.
How much do Squamish councillors get paid?
$46,926 each in 2025 and $44,813 a year at 2026 rates. From 2027 a councillor gets 36% of the mayor's pay, or $45,000.
Is being on Squamish council a full time job?
The District does not say. When council talked about pay in July 2026, members discussed whether the role is full time or part time and whether councillors can keep other jobs, but no rule was set.
Who decides council pay?
Council does, through a bylaw voted on in public. Since December 2025, an outside pay review is funded once every four years, ahead of each election.
Where can I see what each member is paid?
In the District's yearly Statement of Financial Information, which lists each member's pay, expenses and benefits.

question: Why did Squamish property taxes go up 12.8%?
short: Why Squamish property taxes went up 12.8%
answer: The District of Squamish raised the property tax money it collects to run the town by 12.8% for 2026, to $56.1 million. Most of the increase paid for costs it was already committed to, such as staff wages and benefits, RCMP policing, transit, inflation and debt on projects already approved. Council debated the budget in late 2025 and adopted it unanimously on January 13, 2026.

p.t: Both dates come up. Council worked on the budget in late 2025 and adopted the 2026 to 2035 financial plan on January 13, 2026, so the 12.8% increase is on 2026 tax bills. The year before, 2025, taxes for operations went up 12.5%.

sections.h: What it cost a typical property

p.t: The District's 2026 figures for the municipal part of the tax bill. School and regional district taxes are extra.

after.t: Earlier estimates said about $382 or $389 more for the average home. Those were drafts; the figures above are from April 2026, after tax rates were set.

p.t: When staff presented the draft budget on December 9, 2025, it was a 13.1% increase. They broke it down like this (the final increase was 12.8%):

list: About 7.7 points: costs already committed, such as labour and benefit contracts, policing, transit, inflation and debt payments on approved projects.
About 2.9 points: keeping services at their current level, including fire services and transit.
About 2.4 points: money set aside to repair and replace roads, pipes and buildings.
The rest: new or one time projects and community grants.

after.t: Staff said most of the increase came from costs the District could not avoid, not new services. The District's tax notice also lists growing RCMP and fire costs, new housing duties from the Province, debt for new facilities, and building reserves ($25.1 million in 2026).
Armand Hurford, mayor at the time, called the town's shortage of facilities one of the main drivers.

p.t: Utility fees are billed separately. For 2026, sewer (wastewater) fees went up 7.2%, water 1.8% and garbage collection 5.2%.

sections.h: Why the total tax collected rose more than 12.8%

p.t: In spring 2026 the District collected $5.8 million more than planned from Woodfibre LNG, after the plant's assessment jumped. Council put that money into reserves for building projects instead of daily operations, so it did not lower anyone's bill. With it, total municipal taxes for 2026 were $61.9 million.

The 10 year plan expects increases of about 13% in 2027 and 12.9% in 2028, mostly for RCMP contracts, debt payments and more fire staff and transit. Staff's first draft for 2027, shown in September 2026, starts at 10.4% before new items. The new council decides the 2027 budget over the winter.

faq: How much did Squamish property taxes go up in 2026?
The money the District collects for operations went up 12.8%, to $56.1 million. For the average single family home, the municipal part of the bill went up $520, to $4,466.
Why did Squamish raise property taxes so much?

Mostly for costs it was already committed to: wages and benefits, RCMP policing, transit, inflation and debt on approved projects. Smaller parts went to keeping fire and transit service levels and to reserves for repairing roads, pipes and buildings.
Did Woodfibre LNG's taxes lower the increase?
No. The extra $5.8 million from Woodfibre in 2026 went into reserves for building projects, not daily operations.

question: How much does Squamish depend on Woodfibre LNG's taxes?
short: How much Squamish depends on Woodfibre LNG's taxes
answer: Woodfibre LNG paid about 12% of the District of Squamish's municipal property taxes in 2026, up from 3% in 2025, as the plant's assessed value rose while it was built. It is the town's only major industry property. The District puts that extra money into reserves rather than daily operations, so the operating budget does not depend on it.

p.t: Municipal property taxes only, from the District's tax rate reports.

after.t: The District's Woodfibre page says the company paid $7.7 million in 2026. The tax rate report shows $7.24 million levied on its property. Neither explains the difference.

p.t: The plant's assessed value rose 391% from 2025 to 2026 as construction went on, from $11.8 million to $57.9 million. The tax rate stayed the same: $125 for every $1,000 of assessed value for major industry, set in 2024 when Squamish had no property in that class.

For comparison, the District says the average major industry rate in B.C. communities that have one was $31 per $1,000 in 2026. When the pulp mill closed in 2006, the rate on that site was $58 per $1,000 and the mill paid about 16% of the town's municipal taxes.

sections.h: What the District does with it

p.t: District staff wrote that it is best practice not to rely on revenue from a single large business to fund ongoing operations. So the District puts Woodfibre money above what it planned for into reserves for one time spending: $1.5 million in 2025 and $5.8 million in 2026.

sections.h: The rejected deal and the court cases

p.t: Woodfibre has three legal cases against the District over its 2025 and 2026 taxes and other matters. In 2026 the District negotiated a 10 year deal worth at least $142 million: fixed payments of $117 million into a capital reserve, plus municipal taxes capped at $2.5 million a year (rising with inflation from 2028). The deal would have ended the court cases.

Council rejected it 5 to 2 on September 22, 2026. Councillors Andersen and French voted for the deal. So regular property taxation continues and the court cases go ahead. District staff said regular taxes could end up higher or lower than the deal.
The new council sets the 2027 tax rates, including the major industry rate, in spring 2027. It could also try to negotiate a new agreement.

faq: How much tax does Woodfibre LNG pay Squamish?
About $7.2 million in municipal property taxes in 2026 (the District's Woodfibre page says $7.7 million), up from $1.47 million in 2025.
What share of Squamish's taxes comes from Woodfibre LNG?
About 12% of municipal property taxes in 2026, up from 3% in 2025.
Does Squamish's budget depend on Woodfibre LNG?
The District says it is best practice not to rely on one large business for ongoing operations, so it puts Woodfibre money above plan into reserves for one time spending instead.

question: What is happening with Brennan Park Recreation Centre?
answer: Brennan Park just finished a $21 million first round of green and accessibility renovations, but there is still no approved plan, cost estimate or money to expand it or replace it with a second ice rink or a bigger pool. A District staff team called the Recreation Centre Task Force is studying options with consultants, with a final report expected in 2027. The draft 2027 to 2036 capital plan, reviewed October 6, 2026, pays for repairs and an electrical upgrade, not an expansion. Any large borrowing for a new building would first need voter approval.

p.t: The first renovation project at Brennan Park cost $21 million and was declared finished in July 2026. More than three quarters of the work was hidden: a central heat pump system, new ammonia and fire alarm systems, a new rooftop unit, and structural, energy and accessibility work. The parts people see are a renovated lobby, an elevator to a newly accessible second floor with a viewing area over the ice, new change rooms and lockers, universal washrooms, two new program rooms and a covered walkway to the pool entrance.

It was paid for mostly by more than $11.7 million from the federal Green and Inclusive Community Buildings program and $1.2 million from the Build Communities Strong Fund. The District has also secured $10.4 million for a second project on the outside of the building (insulation, windows, doors, earthquake safety and electrical), but no date is set. Officials said that timing waits for the task force findings.

sections.h: The plan to expand or replace it

p.t: In December 2025, the old council put $125,000 for 2026 into the 10 year financial plan to study a Brennan Park upgrade. Councillor Hamilton opposed. A separate motion to spend $200,000 on a feasibility study for a second pool and rink by July 2026 failed, with Mayor Hurford and Councillors French, Andersen and Stoner opposed.

The study is run by the Recreation Centre Task Force, a team of District staff, with Cornerstone Planning Group as the main consultant. It is Phase 1 of three. Phase 1 checks what the community needs, studies the building's condition, electrical service, archaeology and environment, compares options, and produces rough early cost estimates and ways to pay. Staff say the electrical supply at the site is maxed out after the retrofit, which limits any expansion until it is upgraded.

On September 1, 2026, council endorsed the task force's engagement plan. Staff had advised against a council committee and against broad public consultation this round. The plan instead uses interviews with sports clubs, the school district and Squamish Nation talks, plus an online survey for users.

sections.h: What the October 6 capital plan includes

p.t: The draft capital plan covers $357 million of projects over 10 years, with $24.6 million in 2027. It has no money to build a Brennan Park expansion. Staff wrote that the District's borrowing capacity is largely committed to major facility and landfill expansion projects.

According to an unofficial summary of the October 6 meeting, council voted 4 to 2 to show possible Brennan Park upgrade funding in the plan documents (Councillors Hamilton, Stoner, Pettingill and Greenlaw for, French and Andersen against). Staff said there is no cost estimate yet, so any number would not be reliable. We could not find the official minutes yet.

list: Upgrade of the main underground electrical service, so the site can expand later: $1 million ($60,000 in 2027, $940,000 in 2028)
Arena heating, ventilation and air conditioning upgrade: $573,000 in 2027 and 2028, after a 2025 arena shutdown when condensation made the ice unsafe
Splash park: $1.7 million in 2027 and 2028
Field house replacement: about $1 million, mostly in 2028
Accessible playground: about $1.1 million, designed in 2030 and built in 2032
A 2027 study on turning the new second floor room into a fitness centre

after.t: Most of these keep the old building running. The arena sprinkler piping dates to 1977 and a skylight near the pool entrance to 1992; both are set to be replaced.

p.t: The pool, called the Squamish Aquatic Centre, is owned by the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District and run by the District of Squamish. Each year the District sends the regional district a budget request. On September 8, 2026, council approved a 2027 request of $4.777 million: $1.772 million to run the pool and $3.005 million for capital work. Another $1.225 million of capital is planned for 2028.

The 2027 capital money is for replacing the pool's air handling unit (installed in 2013), new plastic lockers, pipes and mechanical equipment, the pool deck, tiles and underground electrical service. Staff wrote that the pool runs at capacity and that staffing has been a challenge since a 2025 health authority pool closure. An unofficial meeting summary says Councillor Pettingill voted against the request over the gas heating, and staff called it the community's only pool.

sections.h: How a new building could be paid for

p.t: No funding plan exists yet. Staff say a project this size would need several sources, such as reserves, grants, partners, developer contributions and borrowing, and that without one main source construction may be phased or scaled back.

In British Columbia, long term municipal borrowing needs approval from voters. Council can use an alternative approval process, where the borrowing goes ahead unless at least 10% of eligible voters sign forms against it within at least 30 days, or it can hold a referendum (called assent voting). If 10% object, council can go to a referendum within 80 days or rethink the plan.
Staff said the borrowing already in the draft plan brings the District's debt servicing (yearly loan payments) to 14%, below its own policy cap of 20% and the provincial cap of 25%.

The new council still has to adopt the 2027 to 2036 financial plan, which an unofficial meeting summary expected in December. The District says a workshop to introduce the plan to the new council and a public information night are coming, with dates to be announced.

sections.h: What the new mayor and council said

p.t: The new council took office on November 3, 2026. At that meeting, Councillor Prosko named Brennan Park as one of the big decisions ahead, and a student guest asked council to make the Brennan Park pool and rink a priority. Here is what each of the seven elected members said during the campaign.

list: Mayor Sean Easton: negotiate with Woodfibre LNG (liquefied natural gas) for a new recreation centre with a pool and ice rink. In his answers to Squamish Voters he said Brennan Park should be paid for by a fair deal with industry, not more public debt.
Sarah Ellis: speed up the task force so a replacement is designed and priced.

Eric Andersen: add a full update of the Parks and Recreation Master Plan alongside the Brennan Park work. He is the only returning member, and on the old council he voted against the $200,000 pool and rink study in December 2025.
Laura Prosko: work toward shovels in the ground for a second ice rink in 2027.
Luc Perreault: hold off on major expansions until there is a clear plan to pay for them.
Janice DesJardins: if a big expansion is proposed, send it to a referendum, not an alternative approval process.
Shaun Veltkamp: lists investing in childcare, recreation and community programs, with no specific Brennan Park plan we could find.

after.t: The old council turned down the 10 year Woodfibre LNG tax deal 5 to 2 on September 22, 2026, and the company's chief executive later called it a fair and final offer. Whether a new deal could include a recreation centre is not known.

faq: Is Brennan Park getting a second ice rink or a new pool?
Not yet. No option has been chosen, priced or funded. The task force's final report with options is expected in 2027, and council would decide after that.
Is Brennan Park closing?

No closure has been announced. The first renovation finished in July 2026, and the 2027 plan pays for repairs to the pool and arena so the building keeps running while the long term plan is worked out.
How much would a new recreation centre cost?
Nobody knows yet. Staff told council on October 6, 2026 that there is no cost estimate, and rough estimates are part of the task force's work.
Will there be a referendum on Brennan Park?

Only if council chooses one. Borrowing needs voter approval, either through an alternative approval process or a referendum. Councillor DesJardins promised to push for a referendum on any big expansion.
How can I have my say?

Watch for the task force survey and the What We Heard report, comment on the 2027 budget at letstalksquamish.ca/budget-2027, or email budgetfeedback@squamish.ca. The District says a budget workshop for the new council and a public information night are coming, with dates still to be announced.
